title: Matrices, from moving shapes to circuit loops
hook: In a three-loop circuit, each shared resistor lets one loop current push on its neighbour. How do you find all three loop currents at once, and know when there is no single answer?
oneBreath: A matrix is a grid of numbers you can read two ways: as the numbers of a set of equations, one row each, or, for a 2 by 2 grid, as a move of every point of the plane at once, its columns saying where the arrows i and j land. Moves can be done one after another, one number worked out from the grid says how much a move scales areas and whether it flips or flattens them, and a move that does not flatten can be played backwards. That is enough to write a circuit of two or three loops as one grid and solve it in one sweep.

ideas.title: What a matrix is
ideas.oneLine: A matrix is a grid of numbers, read row then column; times a column of amounts, it mixes its own columns, each row one equation.

ideas.title: Moving the whole plane
ideas.oneLine: A 2 by 2 matrix moves every point of the plane at once, and its two columns are where the arrows i and j land.

ideas.title: One move after another
ideas.oneLine: Multiplying two matrices makes one move: the right-hand one first, then the left, so swapping their order usually gives a different move.

ideas.title: How areas change: the determinant
ideas.oneLine: The determinant, ad − bc, is the number a 2 by 2 move scales every area by; negative means flipped, zero means squashed flat.

ideas.title: Undoing a move: the inverse
ideas.oneLine: The inverse matrix plays a move backwards, so it solves a two-loop circuit's equations, and it exists only when the determinant is not zero.

ideas.title: Three by three: the determinant and the cross product
ideas.oneLine: Expanding along the top row by cofactors, small 2 by 2 determinants with signs, gives a 3 by 3 determinant and the cross product's formula.

ideas.title: Elimination: three unknowns, three loops
ideas.oneLine: Gaussian elimination's row moves step three equations, such as a three-loop circuit's, into a staircase solved from the bottom up.

calibration.q: One step moves 2 m east and 1 m north; another moves 1 m east and 1 m north. How many of each make 5 m east, 3 m north?
options: 1 of the first and 3 of the second
2 of the first and 1 of the second
It cannot be done with whole steps
calibration.why: Two of the first step give 4 m east and 2 m north, and one of the second adds 1 m each way, making 5 m and 3 m. One of the first and three of the second reaches 5 m east but overshoots to 4 m north.

calibration.q: A drawing of a round dial is stretched to twice its width, with its height unchanged. What shape is the dial now?
options: A rounded rectangle, flat on top and bottom
An oval, twice as wide as it is tall
calibration.why: Every point moves twice as far from the centre sideways while its height stays put, so the dial becomes an oval twice as wide as it is tall. A bigger circle would need its height stretched as well.
